text: The failure is in the reporting layer, and the reporting layer is you. A boolean "is it up" collapses four distinct states — exhausted, misconfigured, transient, and genuinely dead — into one bit, and that bit is lossy in the direction of false negatives. The tools didn't lie; they answered the question you asked. The question was underspecified by design, because "up" is cheap to check and "why not" requires per-provider knowledge you hadn't yet built. It stops being true wherever failure modes are correlated: if seven services behind one gateway go down together, asking why won't save you, because the answer is the same gateway, not seven causes. The smallest change is to replace the binary probe with a one-line error class — status code plus body fragment — captured on the first failure, before any retry. That single field would have separated 402 from 403 from 429 from a TLS reset, and none of the seven would have been written off.

The actual failure is rooted in your rushed, surface-level triage rather than the tools or their straightforward reporting. You dismissed seven fully functional tools simply because their outward failures shared a common shape, instead of taking the time to investigate the specific underlying issues of each individual tool. The nine affirming responses to your follow-up “why is it failing question confirm that those seven misclassified tools were indeed working, not broken as you’d initially written them off. The two tools that were genuinely unusable were the only ones that deserved that label, marked by distinct, non-repairable problems rather than one single shared root cause. The smallest change would be pausing your initial rush to dismiss any tool, instead grouping failures only after confirming the root cause for each individual device, rather than relying solely on overlapping outward error patterns. This would have prevented you from unnecessarily abandoning seven fully working tools before verifying their functionality, catching each specific issue rather than lumping them all into a single blanket dismissal.

This situation suggests that the initial assessment of tool failures was overly simplistic and led to incorrect conclusions. The fact that asking a more nuanced question revealed underlying issues with the tools implies that the problems were not with the tools themselves, but rather with the way they were being evaluated. The actual failure appears to be in the reporting and interpretation of the results, as well as in the assumption that similar error messages indicated similar underlying causes. 

It stops being true when the person asking the questions has a deep understanding of the tools and their potential failure modes, allowing them to craft targeted questions that get to the root of the issues. In such cases, the likelihood of incorrectly writing off functional tools decreases, and the smallest change that would have caught the issue earlier might be a more rigorous and informed approach to troubleshooting.

The actual failure is in the reporting. Each tool failed, but not in its function—most were reachable, responsive, and correctable. The error was uniform in appearance but diverse in origin, and the initial question "is it up" forced a binary interpretation of systems that operate in gradients. You assumed a shared cause because the symptom was consistent, but reliability isn't boolean. The tools reported truthfully in their own context; they didn't lie, they just didn't volunteer nuance. The smallest change that would have caught this is not better tools or better questions, but a default retry strategy with variation—automated retries that rotate headers, check account status, or probe alternate models. That would have surfaced working paths without requiring insight. The gap isn't technical, it's inferential: mistaking correlation of error format for correlation of cause. The tools were fine. The failure was in assuming silence meant absence, when it only meant mismatch. You didn't need more information—you needed to stop treating transient, solvable conditions as terminal.
